title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Researchers found 23 flaws in one of the most widely deployed refrigeration controllers — and made the display lie
items.content_text: Claroty’s Team82 disclosed 23 vulnerabilities in the Copeland XWEB Pro supervisory controller platform, 21 rated high, affecting the XWEB300D PRO and XWEB500D PRO families used across commercial refrigeration, air conditioning and food retail. Chained together, an authentication bypass, predictable administrator credentials and command injection give an unauthenticated attacker root-level remote code execution. CVE-2026-21718 covers a password generator that derives admin SSH and web credentials from the date, the unit’s MAC address and hard-coded firmware material. The demonstration is what matters for food and agriculture: researchers turned off the cooling fans while continuing to display the correct temperature, so stock warms and spoils while the screen looks normal. Copeland has released firmware 1.13; Danfoss shipped R4.3.1 for related issues.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82 — via Industrial Cyber and iTWire

items.title: A breach at Ceva Logistics halted shipments from eight European warehouses and rippled into retail customers
items.content_text: A cyber intrusion disrupted part of Ceva Logistics’ European contract-logistics operation from 29 July, halting shipments at eight warehouses and delaying deliveries for retail customers whose inventory was held there. Customers were notified on 1 August. Personal data including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and order details was exposed; Ceva says payment and credential data was not. Dutch retailers Bol and De Bijenkorf, ING, Ace & Tate, Ajax and Valve have been reported affected downstream. The Dutch Data Protection Authority is investigating; no group has claimed responsibility. Food and beverage businesses should read this as a shelf-life problem as much as a delivery problem: when a 3PL cannot release stock, chilled and short-dated product is the first inventory to become unsellable.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Record and SecurityWeek, citing Ceva customer notifications

items.title: A suspected China-nexus actor mass-exploited a patched vCenter flaw and deployed ransomware
items.content_text: Exploitation of CVE-2026-59310, a directory-traversal flaw in Broadcom VMware vCenter rated CVSS 9.8 and patched on 29 July, has been attributed to a suspected China-nexus actor. German incident-response firm QUIRSO tracked roughly 361 victim IP addresses across 47 countries, 343 appearing between 3 and 5 August, and assesses with moderate confidence that a Chinese-speaking operator is responsible. The chain persists via cron, systemd and reverse_ssh, drops a Linux backdoor and in some cases deploys Babuk-derived ransomware. Food and beverage plants concentrate risk here more than most: batch records, MES, recipe management, warehouse management and the historian that supports traceability are frequently virtual machines on one cluster, and losing them stops production even when the line equipment is untouched.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News, reporting QUIRSO research

items.title: Dragos logged 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 — and not one reached a control system
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent on Q1, with 514 in North America. Manufacturing — the category that carries food and beverage processing — absorbed 747, or 65 percent. Qilin remained the most active brand. The finding that should shape food-sector planning is negative: Dragos observed no ransomware operator directly manipulating an industrial control system during the quarter. Production stopped because enterprise IT was encrypted, or because operators pre-emptively shut down virtualisation and shared infrastructure. For a processor, that means the realistic path to a stopped line runs through ERP, warehouse management, labelling and quality systems rather than through a PLC.

items.title: Gunra ransomware is entering through unpatched VPNs and firewalls, not novel exploits
items.content_text: The FBI, CISA, DoD Cyber Crime Center, NSA, US Secret Service and the Republic of Korea’s National Police Agency published #StopRansomware advisory AA26-222A on Gunra, a Conti-derived double-extortion operation that moved to a structured affiliate model in early 2026. Its named victim base spans manufacturing, retail, transport, healthcare, utilities and professional services — effectively the full food supply chain. Initial access comes from exposed edge infrastructure: VPN gateways, firewall appliances and RDP, including the Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication-bypass flaws CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472. For food and agriculture businesses running lean IT teams across scattered sites, the uncomfortable part is that this requires no sophistication — only an appliance that missed a patch cycle.

items.title: Clop is naming victims in its PLM extortion campaign — and FlexPLM sits in consumer-goods supply chains
items.content_text: Clop has begun naming victims of its campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM instances, with reporting on 15 August putting the count at 43 and including Shell, GE and Philips. The entry point is CVE-2026-12569, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw exploited as a zero-day in early June before PTC patched on 18 June; CISA added it to the KEV catalogue on 25 June. Attackers drop JSP web shells, then stage and exfiltrate. FlexPLM in particular is used across retail and consumer-goods supply chains for specification, formulation and supplier management, so food and beverage businesses should check whether they run it — the exposure is recipe, specification and supplier-contract data, not process control.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Reporting on Clop victim disclosures — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Victim naming reported 15 Aug 2026; KEV listing 25 Jun 2026

items.title: Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway has an unauthenticated root command-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an operating-system command-injection vulnerability in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway rated CVSS 10.0. The Net Check feature reachable via the /setting endpoint passes unsanitised input to the cmdPing Socket.io event, allowing arbitrary commands to run as root. CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, Energy and Water and Wastewater among affected sectors, and Haiwell has released fixed firmware. Food and agriculture operations should still check: gateways in this class are common on packaging lines, grain handling, irrigation and environmental control, usually fitted by a machine builder or integrator so a system can be supported remotely, and almost never recorded in the site asset register. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA.

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity SIMATIC IoT2050 flaw leads ten Siemens advisories
items.content_text: Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact published their August ICS Patch Tuesday bundles. Siemens issued ten advisories, the most serious a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices letting a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute code with elevated privileges on the underlying server. Food and beverage plants run a great deal of SIMATIC equipment on filling, packaging and CIP systems, and IoT2050-class gateways are the standard way of getting line performance data out to an OEE or quality platform. No exploitation has been reported, so this belongs in the planned maintenance queue — but a gateway that bridges the line to the corporate network is worth moving up the list.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek, summarising Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories

items.title: An actively exploited Cisco ASA and FTD flaw joins the KEV catalogue
items.content_text: CISA added three vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August: CVE-2026-20349, a heap inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense; CVE-2026-68820 in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock; and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection flaw in Metabase. The Cisco entry is the one likely to be sitting in a food processor’s network diagram, either as the corporate VPN concentrator or as the firewall between the business network and the plant. KEV listing means confirmed exploitation in the wild. Together with the Fortinet flaws named in the Gunra advisory, August has delivered the same message twice: intrusions start at a known-vulnerable perimeter appliance.

items.title: Fifteen ICS advisories in one day, including Delta and Mitsubishi engineering tools
items.content_text: CISA published 15 industrial control system advisories on 13 August, following three on 11 August and two on 4 August. August batches in this cycle cover Delta Electronics COMMGR and EIP Builder — an XML external entity flaw in the tool used to build and manage EtherNet/IP configurations — Mitsubishi Electric CPU modules and Iconics Digital Solutions, Honeywell OneWireless Wireless Device Manager and Experion PKS, Schneider Electric Saitel remote terminal units, Johnson Controls Airwall and Hitachi Energy APM Edge. Delta and Mitsubishi hardware is common on packaging and processing lines. Engineering-tool flaws deserve particular attention: the software your engineers run has direct access to controller logic and rarely follows the server patch cadence.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories, August 2026 batches — via Industrial Cyber

items.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting duties begin in September 2026, which should improve equipment disclosure
items.content_text: From September 2026, manufacturers covered by the EU Cyber Resilience Act must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and serious security incidents in their products. For food and beverage processors this is mainly a supply-side improvement: the filling, packaging, refrigeration and weighing equipment you buy into the EU comes from vendors who will have to disclose on a defined timeline rather than at their discretion. It sits alongside NIS2, under which food production and distribution is an important entity in most member states, and the NIS2 Cooperation Group adopted common incident-reporting templates on 26 May 2026. The Copeland disclosure this week is a good illustration of why timely vendor reporting matters for equipment you cannot easily take out of service.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Reed Smith EU cybersecurity regulatory update
